claims.text: A high-entropy alloy solid solution contains at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
Solid-solution high-entropy alloys can contain localized pockets of nonrandom atomic distributions called clustered ordering.
Superconducting behavior in an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy is governed by the combination of clustered ordering and high entropy of mixing.
Clustered ordering acts as a structural mediator of superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys.
High entropy of mixing promotes the formation of simple-structure solid-solution phases.
High entropy of mixing suppresses the formation of numerous intermetallic phases.
Iterative transport characterization and density-functional-theory simulation can refine understanding of superconductivity in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed superconducting behavior applies at cryogenic temperatures.
The proposed mechanism applies under high pressure.
The proposed mechanism applies across variable chemical compositions.
The uncharacterized high-entropy alloy will have an increased superconducting critical temperature relative to conventional superconducting materials.
The uncharacterized high-entropy alloy will have an increased upper critical field relative to conventional superconducting materials.
Nb-Ta matrices and titanium-rich systems constitute the baseline conventional superconducting materials.
The relationship among clustered ordering, entropy of mixing, and superconducting properties is not yet fully understood.
Comparing alloys with varying degrees of clustered ordering and entropy of mixing can test the proposed mechanism.
Absence of both the predicted superconducting-property correlation and the expected clustered ordering would falsify the hypothesis.
A 10 percent deviation from predicted values is designated as a falsification threshold.
